explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Jesus says it would be better for the person to have a millstone hung around his neck and be thrown into the sea "…than to cause one of these little ones to stumble." (Luke 17:2) That's a heavy line, so I'll say it plainly and leave it alone. He doesn't tell us here who the little ones are, so I won't guess either.

I get why you'd pick priests, since they sound like sermon material. But priests never come up in these verses. Jesus names "…one of these little ones…" (Luke 17:2). When the text hands you the name, you just pass it along.

Pharisees do show up in plenty of places in Luke, like in Luke 5:30, but not in this warning. Verse 2 doesn't mention them at all. Jesus says it would be better for him to be thrown into the sea "…than to cause one of these little ones to stumble." That's who He names.

Yes, friend, forgive. Jesus puts it in two short steps: "If your brother sins, rebuke him; and if he repents, forgive him." (Luke 17:3) Notice the order. The rebuke comes first, and the forgiveness follows when he repents.
Avoiding someone is easy to do. I've dodged a ringing oven timer that way. But Jesus doesn't say to avoid the brother. He says, "…if he repents, forgive him." (Luke 17:3)

Testing him sounds careful, like poking a cookie to see if it's done. But Jesus never gives a testing step. He says, "…if he repents, forgive him." (Luke 17:3) No quiz is mentioned, just the forgiving.

Seven it is, baker. Jesus says, "Even if he sins against you seven times in a day, and seven times returns to say, ‘I repent,’ you must forgive him." (Luke 17:4) Seven times in one day. That's a lot of tally marks on the oven door, and Jesus still says forgive.

Three feels like plenty to me, and I'd be asking for a break by then. But Jesus gives a bigger number than that. He says "…seven times in a day, and seven times returns to say, ‘I repent,’…" and then "you must forgive him." (Luke 17:4)

Ten is a nice round number, but it's not the one Jesus uses. He says "seven times in a day, and seven times returns to say, ‘I repent.’" (Luke 17:4) It's seven both times in that sentence. And the answer is still "you must forgive him."

That's it, friend. The apostles said to the Lord, "Increase our faith!" (Luke 17:5) The text doesn't say why they asked, but I think that forgiveness talk landed hard. I'd have asked for more of something too.

That's a real request, but it came at a different time. In Luke 11:1, one of His disciples asked Jesus to teach them to pray. Here in Luke 17:5 the apostles say, "Increase our faith!" Different moment, different ask.
That one belongs to Philip, one of Jesus' disciples. He asked Jesus to show them the Father (John 14:8). Here, the apostles say something else to the Lord: "Increase our faith!" (Luke 17:5)

explanations.answer: Faith the size of a mustard seed
explanations.explanation: You've got it, baker. Jesus says, "If you have faith the size of a mustard seed, you can say to this mulberry tree, ‘Be uprooted and planted in the sea,’ and it will obey you." (Luke 17:6) A mustard seed is tiny. Jesus picked it, so I'm not going to argue with Him.

Abraham, Israel's forefather (Matthew 1:2), is a big name, and I see why you reached for it. But he never comes up in these verses. Jesus talks about "…faith the size of a mustard seed…" (Luke 17:6) The size He names is small.

That sounds like a lot to ask of anybody, me included. But Jesus doesn't say anything about never doubting. He says, "If you have faith the size of a mustard seed…" (Luke 17:6) The measure He gives is a seed.

I see why you'd say that, because sitting down sounds right after plowing or shepherding. But the master in Jesus' picture says something else. He tells the servant, "Prepare my meal and dress yourself to serve me while I eat and drink, and afterward you may eat and drink…" (Luke 17:8) So the answer is False.

That's right, baker. If you were picturing the servant pulling up a chair, Jesus' picture says not yet. The master says, "Prepare my meal and dress yourself to serve me while I eat and drink, and afterward you may eat and drink…" (Luke 17:8) The servant does get his meal, but afterward, and that order is how Jesus sets it up.

Yes, serve! The master says, "Prepare my meal and dress yourself to serve me while I eat and drink…" (Luke 17:8) Notice the order, baker. Dress yourself first, like me tying on my apron before anybody touches a cookie, then serve. The servant's own turn to eat comes afterward.
Guarding sounds sharp, like standing at the cookie jar with my mustache folded. But the master doesn't say guard. He says, "…dress yourself to serve me while I eat and drink…" (Luke 17:8)

Leaving would be a nice break, I'll give you that. But the master doesn't send him away. He says, "…dress yourself to serve me while I eat and drink, and afterward you may eat and drink…" (Luke 17:8) The servant stays and serves first.

explanations.answer: The servant only did his job
explanations.explanation: That's the point, friend. Jesus asks, "Does he thank the servant because he did what he was told?" (Luke 17:9) It's a question, and the picture gives its answer. Then verse 10 ends with "we have only done our duty."

A reward would be nice, and I'd frame it on the wall. But Jesus' question points the other direction. He asks, "Does he thank the servant because he did what he was told?" (Luke 17:9) Nothing about a reward comes up in these verses.

explanations.answer: The servant deserves a day off
explanations.explanation: A day off sounds wonderful, I haven't had one in a while. But a day off isn't in this picture. Jesus only asks, "Does he thank the servant because he did what he was told?" (Luke 17:9) The master tells him to serve, and then the servant may eat and drink.

That's what Jesus says. "So you also, when you have done everything commanded of you, should say, ‘We are unworthy servants; we have only done our duty.’…" (Luke 17:10) It's a humble line. The servant picture from verses 7 to 9 leads right to it.

Faithful is a lovely word, and it sounds like something to put on a cookie box. But it's not what Jesus tells them to say. He says, "We are unworthy servants; we have only done our duty." (Luke 17:10)

I can see how verse 9 could point you there, since it mentions thanks. But Jesus' question there is, "Does he thank the servant because he did what he was told?" The words He gives the disciples are different. They are to say, "We are unworthy servants; we have only done our duty." (Luke 17:10)
